Minute fifty-one. A goal with the hand. The referee doesn't see it.
Minute fifty-five. The same player. Sixty metres, six opponents... and the most beautiful goal in World Cup history.
The most dishonest goal... and the most beautiful goal. Same guy. Same match. Four minutes apart.
This is the story of how a team everyone laughed at, and a player who stood five foot five... conquered the world. And why, forty years later, the whole planet is still watching that match.
To understand Mexico, you have to go back a year. June thirtieth, nineteen eighty-five, River Plate's stadium. Last day of the qualifiers: Argentina against Peru.
A draw would send Argentina to the World Cup. But with ten minutes left... they were losing two to one. And the whole country was ten minutes away from being left out.
Passarella shoots, the ball hits the post... and Ricardo Gareca pounces on the rebound. Two-two. Argentina is going to the World Cup. Through the back door.

The coach was Carlos Bilardo. And everybody criticised Bilardo: the press, the fans, even the seventy-eight world champions. They said his team played ugly football. That it couldn't beat anyone. There was even a push to sack him... weeks before the World Cup.
But Bilardo had one fixed idea: the whole team would play for one man. And he gave that man the captain's armband. Diego Armando Maradona. Twenty-five years old.

He arrived in Mexico as the biggest star in the world. He played for Napoli, in Italy, and his transfer had been the most expensive in history. But at World Cups he owed football one: in Spain eighty-two they had kicked him all over the pitch... and he was sent off.

And there was one more problem. The squad's other great leader, the captain of the seventy-eight champions, Daniel Passarella, fell ill in Mexico... and didn't play a single minute. The team was Diego's. For better or worse.
First match, at the Olympic University Stadium: South Korea. The Koreans had one plan for Diego... kick him. They fouled him eleven times in ninety minutes.
But Argentina won three to one. Two goals from Jorge Valdano... and one from Oscar Ruggeri. All three set up by Diego.
Then, in Puebla, the world champions: Italy. Altobelli, from the spot, one-nil. And Maradona, from almost no angle, left-footed... one-one.
And to finish, Bulgaria: two-nil, goals from Valdano and Burruchaga. Top of the group. Unbeaten. And still, nobody was scared of Argentina.
In the round of sixteen, back in Puebla, the River Plate derby: Uruguay. A tight, cagey match... settled by Pedro Pasculli, just before half-time. One-nil.
But that match left a problem. Argentina had played in thick blue cotton shirts... and in the Mexican heat they weighed a ton. The players finished soaked.

And next, in the quarter-finals, came England, who play in white. Three days before the match, Bilardo sent an assistant, Rubén Moschella, around the shops of Mexico City. To look for shirts... in a store.

He came back with two models. Maradona picked one and said: with this one, we beat England. They bought thirty-eight, sewed on the crest... and ironed silver numbers on the back, the kind used in American football. That's the shirt in the most famous photo of the century.

Because this was no ordinary match. Four years earlier, Argentina and England had gone to war over the Falklands. Seventy-four days. Six hundred and forty-nine Argentine soldiers dead. Two hundred and fifty-five British.

The players said it was just football. Nobody believed them. And in football there was also unfinished business from sixty-six: at Wembley, Rattín was sent off and refused to leave the pitch... and the England manager called the Argentines animals.
June twenty-second, at noon, under the Mexican sun. The Azteca Stadium: one hundred and fourteen thousand people. The most charged match in World Cup history.
First half: nil-nil. England closed every path. And every time Diego got the ball, he had two Englishmen on him.

Minute fifty-one. Maradona drives through the middle and looks for Valdano. Steve Hodge, the Englishman, tries to clear... and hooks it back towards his own keeper. Out comes Peter Shilton, almost eight inches taller. Diego jumps... and punches it in with his left hand.
Seen from above, it makes more sense. Hodge lifts it backwards. Shilton comes out with both hands. And Diego, who stands five foot five, gets there first... with his fist tucked against his head.
The referee, Tunisia's Ali Bin Nasser, doesn't see it. Goal. The English protest... and Diego shouts to his teammates: come and hug me, or he won't give it.
That night, Maradona would say the goal was scored a little with his head... and a little with the hand of God. Shilton never forgave him. Forty years later, he still hadn't shaken his hand.
Four minutes later, the other thing happened.

Minute fifty-five. Héctor Enrique gives it to Maradona in his own half. He turns, and leaves Beardsley and Reid behind. He's off. Past the halfway line. Butcher comes out: beaten. Fenwick comes out: beaten. Into the box, Shilton comes out... Diego feints, sits him down... and with Butcher hanging off his back, he slides it in. Goal.

Seen from above, it's even crazier. He starts in his own half. Beardsley. Reid. Past the halfway line. Butcher. Fenwick. Into the box. Shilton... and Butcher again. Sixty metres. Ten point eight seconds. And not a single touch with his right foot.

On the radio, Víctor Hugo Morales screamed it for eternity: cosmic kite, what planet did you come from? Enrique, the man who gave him the pass, said afterwards: with the pass I gave him, it was the least he could do. And Gary Lineker, the England striker, confessed it was the only time in his career he felt like applauding an opponent's goal.

In two thousand and two, in a FIFA vote, it was named the goal of the century. The cheat and the genius. Same day, four minutes apart. And maybe that's why, forty years later, we still can't stop watching it.
Lineker pulled one back in the eighty-first minute. But it was too late. Argentina two, England one. On to the semi-finals.
And there was still a final to play. If you like these stories, subscribe to Los Once: this is where we tell all of football, the way it deserves to be told.

In the semi-finals, Belgium. The surprise of the tournament, fresh from knocking out the Soviet Union and Spain. And Diego did it again. Minute fifty-one: he gets between two defenders and chips it over the keeper.
Minute sixty-three. He starts from the left, hugging the touchline. One Belgian is left on the ground. Another, run past. Out comes the keeper, Pfaff... and Diego slots it across him. Again.
Two-nil. Argentina, into the final. Unbeaten: five wins and a draw. And one single name in every newspaper in the world.

June twenty-ninth. The Azteca Stadium, full again. In the other corner, West Germany, coached by Franz Beckenbauer, who had knocked out Platini's France in the semi-finals. Rummenigge, Völler, Schumacher... and Lothar Matthäus, with a single mission: to chase Maradona all over the pitch.
Bilardo picked his usual men. Pumpido in goal. At the back, Cuciuffo, Brown and Ruggeri. In midfield, Giusti, Batista, Enrique and Olarticoechea. Up front, Burruchaga, Valdano... and Diego.

Minute twenty-three: Burruchaga's free kick from the right. Schumacher, the keeper, comes to claim it... and gets stuck halfway. And José Luis Brown, who had never scored for the national team, heads it into the empty net. One-nil.
In that same match, Brown dislocated his shoulder. He tore a hole in his shirt, hooked his finger through it to hold his arm up... and played on. He wasn't going to leave a World Cup final.
Minute fifty-five: Enrique to Valdano, who runs in alone and slots it across. Two-nil. It looked over.
But Germany never gave up. Two corners, two goals. Minute seventy-four: Rummenigge. Minute eighty: Völler. Two-two. And the Azteca... fell silent.
Minute eighty-four. Maradona, surrounded by Germans, lifts his head... and threads a pass to Burruchaga. Who runs, and runs, with Briegel chasing... and slides it past Schumacher. Three-two.

Look at the pass. Diego has three Germans on him, in the centre circle. He lifts his head once. And drops it in front of Burruchaga, forty metres, with a single touch. Briegel runs, but can't get there. The best player in the world, in the eighty-fourth minute of a final... did the simplest thing.
Six minutes later, the Brazilian referee Romualdo Arppi Filho ends the match. Argentina are champions of the world.
Diego lifts the cup at the Azteca. Five goals, five assists... and the tournament's Golden Ball. Never had a player won a World Cup so alone. And it never happened again.
When they got back to Buenos Aires, they came out onto the balcony of the Casa Rosada. And Diego lifted the cup in front of a packed Plaza de Mayo.
Bilardo, the man everyone wanted sacked, was a world champion. With the ugly team. With the team that couldn't beat anyone.

And the blue shirt, the one bought in a shop in Mexico City? After the match, Diego swapped it with Steve Hodge, the Englishman from the clearance. Hodge kept it for thirty-six years. In two thousand twenty-two he auctioned it... for more than nine million dollars. The most expensive shirt in the history of sport.

Forty years went by. Argentina became champions again in Qatar, with Messi. But Mexico eighty-six... will always be Diego's World Cup. The one with the hand. The one with the goal. The one with the four minutes.
